title: Molina need not reconcile efficacy with freedom: grace is subject to choice
source_text: LXXXIV. Hinc patet nullo modo Molinae laborandum esse, ut efficaciam gratiae divinae cum arbitrii humani libertate conciliet. Siquidem Dei gratiam libero hominis arbitrio subjicit; nec vult ullum ejus auxilium esse tantae efficacitatis, ut liberum arbitrium ad agendum ex se determinet; sed qualecunque Dei auxilium ad bonam actionem praevium supponatur, cum eo semper stare posse voluntatis humanae dissensum, & in hominis potestate manere illo pro libitu uti, vel non uti.
pass_a_gloss: LXXXIV. Hence it is plain that Molina need in no way labour to reconcile the efficacy of divine grace with the liberty of human choice. Since he subjects the grace of God to the free choice of man; nor does he will any help of it to be of such efficacy, that it determines free choice to acting of itself; but whatever help of God prior to a good action be supposed, with it the dissent of the human will can always stand, and it remains in man's power to use it at pleasure, or not use it.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXXIV. Plainly, then, Molina has no need to labour at reconciling the efficacy of divine grace with the freedom of human choice. He makes God's grace subject to man's free choice, and will not allow any aid of grace to be so efficacious that it determines free choice to act of itself.
Whatever aid from God is supposed to precede a good action, the human will's dissent can always coexist with it, and it remains in a person's power to use it as he pleases or not to use it.
